me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “always”. It describes something as continually true, regularly present, or applicable at all times. As an adverb, it tells when or how consistently something is done, felt, or remains so. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, showing a consistent sense of ongoing or repeated duration rather than a single moment. Its exact force in a verse comes from the action or statement it modifies. [p03:word:greek-nt:G0104:identity; p03:word:greek-nt:G0104:occurrences]

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “out of season” or “unseasonably”. It describes something done at a time that may seem inconvenient, unexpected, or not naturally suited to the moment. In its single New Testament occurrence, it functions as an adverb, telling how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word appears in 2 Timothy 4:2, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific force there. Its central idea remains acting or speaking without waiting for what might seem like the most suitable time.

me: Adjective, Accusative, Plural, Feminine, NUmerical Indiclinable (A)

e.t: This word means “another,” referring to a different person or thing from one already mentioned or understood. It can identify an additional individual, object, or alternative, helping distinguish one from another within a sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 155 times across 137 verses, so it is a common word for expressing distinction or addition. Its exact reference—who or what is meant by “another”—depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “deceit” or “deception”: misleading influence or conduct that leads someone away from what is true. It can describe the deceptive power of worldly concerns, false teaching, or a hardened heart. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times in seven verses, showing that the word is used in several warnings about influences that mislead people rather than strengthen faithfulness. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

me: Verb, Imperfect, Active, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to lick.” It describes using the tongue to touch or consume something, and it expresses a specific physical action rather than a broad feeling or idea. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 16:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of licking.

e.t: This word means “to turn away” or “to turn away from” someone or something. It describes a change of direction in which a person no longer faces, follows, or remains with what was previously before them. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, so its basic sense is used in several settings without changing its central idea: withdrawal or redirection away from a person, place, or course. The surrounding verse determines what is being left or rejected in each occurrence.

Asher is a personal name referring to a member of the tribe of Asher. In the Greek New Testament, it appears as the name “Asher,” preserving the identity of the person or tribal ancestor being mentioned rather than describing an action or quality. The name occurs twice in this corpus, once in Luke and once in Revelation. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

e.t: This word means “Galatian,” describing someone or something associated with Galatia. It functions as a regional identifier rather than expressing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts: Acts 16:6 and Acts 18:23. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise reference in each passage cannot be explained further, but its central meaning remains a connection with Galatia or its people.

e.t: This word means “to marry” or “marrying”—to enter into marriage. It describes the act of taking or entering a spouse and can refer either to the decision to marry or to the ongoing practice of marrying. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 28 times, appearing in teaching about marriage, remarriage, family life, and ordinary human activity. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This word means “to disperse”—to scatter or break apart so that people or things are no longer gathered together. It is a verb describing an action, not a person or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 5:36. Since the word appears only there and the verse text is not included here, its broader lexical sense is clear, while the precise force of the action depends on the surrounding passage. The central idea remains separation from a gathered or united state.

e.t: This word means “to penetrate”—to pass into or through something rather than remain only on the surface. It describes movement that reaches inward or all the way through. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 4:12. The word’s basic sense is therefore focused and specific: entering deeply or passing through. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

e.t: This word means “to give”: to place something in another person’s possession or provide it for them. It describes an act of giving rather than merely having or receiving. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, including passages in Mark and 2 Peter. Its precise force in any one sentence depends on what is being given and who receives it.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to exclude” or “to alienate”—to shut someone out, keep someone apart, or separate them from a group or relationship. It can also describe something as being excluded. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 3:27 and Galatians 4:17. Its central idea is deliberate separation: someone is prevented from belonging, participating, or remaining connected. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “help”: assistance given to someone who needs support. It describes aid that enables a person to continue or accomplish what would otherwise be difficult. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 26:22, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word points to practical support rather than an abstract idea, and its precise force in Acts depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “appeared” or “to appear”: it describes someone or something becoming visible, coming into view, or being made plainly present. It is an action word, focusing on the arrival or manifestation of what was previously unseen or not openly present. It occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, including passages in Luke, Acts, and Titus. The exact force in any verse depends on what or whom the surrounding passage says appeared.

Hermogenes is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than describing a quality, action, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in 2 Timothy 1:15, and English translations retain it as “Hermogenes.” Because it is a proper name, its ordinary function is to identify the person named; its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

This word means “zeal”: strong, passionate eagerness directed toward a person, cause, or pursuit. It describes an intensity that can be commendable when rightly directed, yet harmful when mixed with rivalry, hostility, or misguided devotion. In the New Testament, it can describe religious earnestness, opposition stirred by jealousy, or intense personal commitment. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that it can describe both devoted action and troubled human passion; the surrounding passage determines whether its force is praiseworthy or destructive.

This word means “altar,” referring to a designated place where offerings are presented to God. In the Greek New Testament, it is used for the altar associated with worship, sacrifice, and sacred service. The word occurs 23 times in the New Testament, appearing especially in Matthew and Revelation, but its basic meaning remains consistent: an altar as the place connected with offering and worship. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Moisture refers to wetness or liquid present in something. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Luke 8:6, and its meaning remains focused and concrete. It identifies the dampness or liquid being described, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular setting. Because the verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from the wording and context of Luke 8:6. Its central meaning is simply moisture: wetness present where it is being described.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “well” or “rightly,” describing something done properly, appropriately, or in a good way. It can affirm that an action or statement is correct, commend the quality of what someone has done, or describe proper conduct. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 36 times, so its exact force depends on the sentence in which it appears. Its central idea remains positive: something is done well, correctly, or as it ought to be.

This word means “gardener,” referring to a person who cares for or works with a garden. It is a noun naming someone by this occupation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at John 20:15. That single occurrence identifies the person by his work, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain the particular situation and significance. Its ordinary meaning remains straightforward: a gardener is someone associated with tending or managing a garden.

This word refers to a cliff or steep bank—a sharply rising or falling edge of land. It describes a physical feature of the landscape rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, each in a different Gospel account. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its basic meaning remains a steep landform or drop-off.

e.t: This word refers to a Cyprian, a person from the island of Cyprus. It functions as a descriptive name for someone’s place of origin rather than as a general description of character or conduct. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Acts. The word is associated with people identified by their connection to Cyprus, so its central meaning is simply “Cyprian” or “from Cyprus.” The surrounding verse is needed to show what each particular person was doing or why the identification mattered.

e.t: This word means “to affirm” or “to reaffirm”—to confirm something as established, valid, or firmly settled. It expresses a strengthening or renewed confirmation rather than a casual statement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Corinthians 2:8 and Galatians 3:15. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains clear: confirming something so that its standing is recognized and upheld.

me: Verb, Aorist, Middle, Subjunctive, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to ransom” or “to redeem”—to act so that someone is released or recovered. It is an action word describing deliverance through redemption, rather than merely naming a condition of freedom. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, including passages about Christ’s saving work and people being redeemed. Its precise emphasis in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context. The word is rendered “redeem” in all three recorded occurrences.

e.t: This word means “to glorify” or “to magnify.” It describes speaking or acting in a way that gives someone honor and causes greatness to be recognized. In the New Testament, it is used of magnifying God, as well as of people or events being publicly honored. The word occurs eight times in the Greek New Testament, so its central idea is consistent while the surrounding passage identifies whom or what is being magnified.

e.t: This word means “to divide” or “to give.” It can describe separating something into portions, or the act of giving something to another. The surrounding sentence determines which sense is intended. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 14 times, so it is used in more than one setting while retaining this basic idea of distributing or granting something. Its recorded usage extends from Matthew through Hebrews.

Nahor is a personal name, referring to a man in the genealogy recorded in the Greek New Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual concept; it identifies a particular ancestor by name. The name occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 3:34. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name itself can be understood simply as the designation of that person within the genealogy.

This word means “child” and can refer to one child or to children as a group. It is a noun used for a young person, with the basic idea remaining the same wherever it appears. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 15 times in 11 verses, showing that it is a recurring word for children rather than a rare or specialized term. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “eighty,” the number equal to eight groups of ten. It functions as a number word, identifying a quantity rather than describing a person, action, or quality. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Luke. Its basic meaning is precise and stable; the surrounding sentence determines what the quantity measures, but the word itself simply states the number eighty.

e.t: This word means “to clothe” or “to dress,” describing the act of putting clothing around someone or oneself. It can refer simply to being dressed or to providing clothes for another person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 23 times, including passages that speak of people being dressed and of clothing others. Its basic sense remains practical and direct: to put on clothing or furnish someone with clothing. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on the person wearing the clothes or the person supplying them.

This word means “bitter,” describing something sharp, unpleasant, or lacking sweetness. It can refer to a literal taste, but in James it is also used for an inward attitude marked by bitterness. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in James 3. Its basic sense remains the same whether it describes what is tasted or the harmful disposition expressed by a person. The surrounding verse determines how the word’s bitterness is being portrayed in a particular passage.

The word means “from Pontus.” It identifies a person or thing by connection with Pontus, functioning as a place-of-origin description rather than naming an action, quality, or object by itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 18:2, so its normal lexical sense is especially focused and straightforward: it marks association with that place. The surrounding verse is needed to explain how the description applies there.

This word refers to a piece of cloth, such as a separate patch or scrap used as material. Its basic sense is concrete and ordinary: it names the cloth itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, in Matthew 9:16 and Mark 2:21. Both references use the same basic idea of a cloth piece, while the surrounding verse determines how that piece functions in the sentence. The word therefore points to a distinct bit of fabric, not to clothing in general.

Semein is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea, action, quality, or object. It is preserved as a name instead of being translated into an English concept. In the Greek New Testament, Semein occurs once, at Luke 3:26. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes the person being named, rather than describing that person’s character or role.

This word refers to an “assassin” or “terrorist”—a person associated with violent attacks. It functions as a noun naming people by that role, not as a general word for opposition, unrest, or conflict. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 21:38. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s particular force in that sentence cannot be expanded safely. Its central meaning remains a violent attacker identified as an assassin or terrorist.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “nearly,” describing something that comes close to happening or being complete but does not quite reach that point. It functions as an adverb, modifying an action, condition, or statement by showing that it is close to fulfillment rather than fully realized. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Acts and Hebrews. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what the surrounding words identify as nearly accomplished or nearly true.

Tarsus is the name of a city, so this word identifies a place rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, all in Acts, and is rendered “Tarsus.” The name is associated with the city connected with Saul’s background and later movements, but the word itself simply names that location. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, while its basic meaning remains the place-name “Tarsus.”

The word is the personal name “Tiberius.” It identifies a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 3:1, so its basic meaning is straightforward. As a personal name, it is not normally translated by a descriptive English word; it is carried over as “Tiberius.” Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the historical setting described there.

This word refers to a table, or to tables when more than one is meant. It names a tangible table in the New Testament and can describe the tables connected with ordinary meals or public activity. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in 14 verses, so its meaning is established across several Gospel and later New Testament passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its English renderings are “table” and “tables.”

e.t: This word means “to endure”—to bear something difficult without giving up. It describes continuing through pressure, suffering, or testing rather than escaping it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, including references to enduring temptation, persecution, and unjust treatment. The word focuses on steadfastly carrying what is difficult. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains patient endurance under hardship.

This word refers to “benevolence” or “love”—a quality of warm, gracious concern for others. It names an inward disposition rather than a specific action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, in Acts 28:2 and Titus 3:4. These meanings point to the central idea of treating others with genuine care. The surrounding verse determines how this quality is expressed in each passage.

e.t: The word means “to buy”—to obtain something by paying for it. It describes an action, telling what someone did rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 7:16. Its basic sense points to obtaining something through payment. The surrounding verse determines what was bought and how the action functions in that sentence, but the word itself identifies the act of buying.
